Browne Lake is a popular destination for campers, glampers, fishermen and hikers.

Just after we turn onto this road, we see in the long meadow to our right another Trailhead, but very importantly see a historical marker--as coming down this meadow we have been paralleling the route of the CARTER MILITARY ROAD, constructed in 1881 and used until 1924 that had the purpose of traveling between Fort Bridger and the railroad on the north to supply military outposts in the Uintah Basin. It followed one of the two routes used by the Native Americans to cross the Uinta Mountains--the other one being up the Henrys Fork, over Gun Sight Pass to the Uinta River Drainage and down to the basin. But, the Carter route made possible supply wagons--even though the distance of 60 miles still was a long torturous trip with a wagon. The story of the Carter Military Road is told on page 474.

This chance visit led to intensive research, explorations and discoveries, and even evolved into me giving speeches on the subject to Historical Societies in Evanston, Wyoming and Coalville, Utah. THANKS TERESA AND BOB!

PREFACE My Struggle to get to Crow Canyon & SURVIVING A FALL & LIGHTNING AT JACKSON PARK Back in 2011, in my zeal to explore and photograph all of the Uintas, I discovered on my NG Wilderness Map what the DWR described as "the smallest drainage on the South Slope ……divided into two main basins: Heller and Crow." 118 The CROW BASIN, "long and narrow with steep side walls," like a box canyon, and basically without marked trails, attracted me most, and in that year I did my first explorations at a time when I was beginning to have a difficult time….actually becoming a cripple, that led in 2012 to my first back surgery fusing vertebras and trying to solve a pinched nerve problem. So 2012 became a year when I was not able to backpack. But my attempts in 2011 did result in one YouTube video about Crow Basin, entitled, "SAW IT, SURVIVED IT"119 but did not tell the whole story. What did come out of that effort was that one of my High Uinta Friends, Jonathan Jaussi, flew over the area and took aerial photographs and shared them with me. They ended up being a great help to me finally getting down into Crow Canyon in 2013, after sort of recovering from my back surgery. That resulted in my 2nd YouTube video, 120 done during Utah's PIONEER DAY CELEBRATION, my trip honoring my great grandmother, Alice Brooks, survivor of the Martin Handcart Company ordeal.

name: Dry Canyon & Fish Lake Trail

ABES (W-30): You get to the lake by following the Middle Fork Trail south from Holiday Park about 2.5 miles to the junction with the Abes Lake Trail and continue one steep mile east to the lake located at 9,820 ft. elevation, 21.6 acres, 62' deep, with a dam so it fluctuates 7 ft. annually, no feed for horses, has Cutthroat and Tiger trout with heavy fishing pressure.

ADAX (W-34): It is a scenic lake at the foot of steep ledges and surrounded by dense conifers. It is accessed by following the Middle Fork Trail south from Holiday Park 2.5 miles and then one steep mile west on an indistinct trail. Another way to get to the lake is 1.5 miles east of Olsen Lake over the pass--no trail. Either way it is difficult to locate in steep, rocky terrain, horse feed is available. Fishing pressure is light for small wild brook trout.

LAKE W-59: It is a natural lake located 1/2 mile southwest of Adax Lake in the Middle Fork Drainage. It can also be accessed from over the ridge from Gardner's Fork but the terrain is of bedrock shelves and scattered conifers and is extremely rough with no trails, horse access is difficult. Located at 10,140 ft. elevation, 4 acres, 10' deep, with a small population of self-sustaining wild brook trout, very light fishing pressure.

Lower DG-26: Meadow lake covered with aquatic vegetation, access from Upper Lily Pad Lake, then 1/8th mile due east. 10,275 ft. elevation, 9 acres, 11 ' deep, Brook trout, light pressure.

The EAST FORK OF BEAR RIVER TRAILHEAD Four lakes are accessed from this trailhead: Off trail Lake Lorena just outside of the Wilderness Area, then a little further along the stream divides: The Right Hand Fork leading to Norice and Priord Lakes; The Left Hand Fork leading to Allsop Lake. NOW FOR THE FEHR LAKE TRAILHEAD, between the Bald Mountain Pass and Mirror Lake, where we will pick up also Marshall Lake from the Murdock Basin.

FEHR (Z-7): This is a natural meadow lake in thick timber at the foot of Murdock Mountain, at 10,260 ft. elevation, 5.7 acres, 27' deep, with a large population of brook trout, under heavy pressure as it is a popular lake.

SHEPARD (Z-9): It is a natural lake surrounded by confers, located 1 mile from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, at 9,980 ft. elevation, 14.2 acres, 32' deep, horse feed is restricted, it has a small population of brook, cutthroat and rainbow trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

MABA (Z-8): Located at the head of Murdock Basin, east of Shepard Lake, and 50 yard north of Hoover Lake, 75 yards west of the Murdock Basin Road, is a natural lake at 9,900 ft. elevation, 4.2 acres, 20' deep with a small population of brook trout, with heavy fishing pressure.

HOOVER (Z-10): This natural lake is surrounded by conifers with some open shoreline, 1.5 miles from the Fehr Lake Trailhead, 50 yards south of Maba Lake, 8 miles northeast of U-150 on the Murdock Basin Road to the Hoover Lake turnoff, the lake found 100 yards northwest of this point. Has brook and cutthroat trout with heavy fishing pressure.

Section 11: The HENRYS FORK TRAILHEAD I must add here, for those who perhaps are new to the Uintas, the HENRYS FORK TRAILHEAD is the main access point to climb Utah's highest mountain--KINGS PEAK, 13,528 ft. high. I must begin this section, with a picture of Kings Peak, and a wonderful historical note about a young 11 year old girl's climb of Kings Peak--actually her 3rd, but I think you'll agree it was AMAZING to say the least. I'll get to driving directions--next page.

:

One day in early July 2018, 11 year old Grace, and her father Jake Hirschi, decided to take advantage of the great weather and climb King's Peak, seen in the exact center of the picture. Grace zeroed in on it and then left her father in her trail dust!106

She climbed it the first time in 2016, when I met them on the trail, me returning from my successful climb to Little Andy Lake. That's when I was honored by her and her brother, Isaac, calling me their “trail buddy”….so all of us became TRAIL BUDDIES.107

I'm not sure at what time they made it to the peak, but after making it and taking a picture, they turned around and headed for the Trailhead, fueled by, I think it was 6 bags of special trail-mix, getting to their car by 8:00 PM that same day--28 miles. WOW! 106

Photos courtesy of Jake Hirschi

From here we can access at least 15 lakes, but I'm recalling that I promised to tell you about one of my adventures when we got to this area. I joke about it as my:

It was in 2016 when I came here with the specific intention of completing my record of climbing all of the 22 passes in the Wilderness Area. From here I wanted to bag 11,360 ft. Fox-Queant Pass, and 12,226 foot North Pole Pass. It was actually my first experience backpacking in the Eastern Uintas, as over the years I had focused mainly on the High Uintas Wilderness Area. I first noticed what seemed like more use of horses. Second, almost everybody was armed with pistols and revolvers, one with a powerful .454 Casull Taurus Raging Bull revolver. His concern wasn't bears as was the case with most, but rather with cougars. I haven't heard of such attacks, so I'm not sure how justified they were, but who knows? I guess carrying makes us all feel like badasses! At Cleveland Lake I had some good fishing, and got a shot or two of bull moose feeding in the lake.

name: Yellow Pine
info: NOW THE WEBER RIVER DRAINAGE The Weber River is a large drainage system on the western extremity of the Uinta Mountains. There are 59 natural lakes and 80+ ponds of less than 2 acres. Eleven of these lakes have been enlarged by dam construction for water storage purposes. Access is provided by Highway 213 east of Oakley and Highway U-150 east of Kamas, Utah. Starting points along Highway 213 include the Erickson Basin Trailhead in the vicinity of the Ledgefork Campground. Other trails originate from Holiday Park but it is on private property and the Forest Service right-of-way road has no trailhead development or parking. NOTE: We will deal with the Trailheads on the Weber River after we examine first those along the Mirror Lake Highway. The major access points to the Weber Drainage are scattered along UT-150 and include the Upper Setting Trailhead, the Crystal lake Trailhead, the Bald Mountain Trailhead, and the Weber River Trail near Pass Lake. Trails originating at these points drop over the top into the major headwater regions of the Weber Basin. Some of the more inaccessible lakes in the Uinta Mountains lie within this drainage. Forest Service trails are not well developed or maintained with the exception of the Notch Mountain Loop Trail, the Lofty Lake Loop Trail, the Smith-Morehouse Trail, and the Yellow Pine Trail.
